key_finding: Shrouding the autopay-minimum-payment option cut the share of cardholders paying exactly the minimum by 23% after six months but did not reduce credit-card debt, and reduced autopay enrollment increased missed payments.
methodology: Field experiment (nudge) on live credit-card accounts with six-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the 'default enrollment = better outcomes' assumption: a nudge that shifted enrolment behavior did not translate into the intended financial benefit, and reduced auto-enrollment increased costly errors — exactly the support team's worry about our round-up defaults.
limitations: Credit-card debt-repayment context, not a savings product
No measure of outcomes beyond 6 months
relevance_reason: Consumer, self-directed financial-app setting testing a default/nudge that changes enrollment but not the outcome that matters, matching the brief's central worry.

key_finding: Synthesizes evidence that automatic enrollment and default investment options raise short-term participation but can reduce longer-term participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative state-of-the-art review of defined-contribution plan design research. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a broad, up-to-date synthesis of the engagement-cost side of defaults that the brief's counter-argument echoes, useful context even though the underlying studies are employer-plan based.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
No quantitative effect sizes in the abstract
Not a systematic review
relevance_reason: Recent overview of the exact default-effect vs engagement trade-off the brief asks about, in the nearest large literature.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment raises short-term participation but induces passivity (low contribution rates, inattentive accounts, churn) that undermines welfare gains unless paired with auto-escalation and re-enrollment prompts.
methodology: Narrative policy commentary, no new data. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Echoes the support team's disengagement concern and suggests mitigations (auto-escalation, reminders) that could apply to a round-up multiplier design.
limitations: US employer retirement system, not consumer fintech
No empirical data or effect sizes
Zero citations, unvetted venue
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the passive-enrollment-vs-engagement trade-off central to the entry-design decision, despite being in the pension domain.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework showing downstream default effects depend on the time course of choice/consumption, prior preferences, and salience of trade-offs, and are not uniform or guaranteed to persist.
methodology: Conceptual synthesis and research-agenda paper drawing on the choice-architecture literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a framework for predicting when a default's initial enrollment effect will or won't persist into real engagement, and flags what to measure (time course, preference antecedents) to test it in-app before committing to opt-out.
limitations: Conceptual/theoretical, not a specific empirical estimate
Not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: A 2025 synthesis of exactly the persistence-of-default-effects question the brief foregrounds, in a general consumer setting.

key_finding: Default enrollment in Medicare Part D has large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is highly insensitive to the value of the default option, even when it causes substantial losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options among low-income Medicare beneficiaries.
why_it_matters: Shows a default effect can persist for a long time and stay large even when against the person's interest, a strong caution against assuming passivity is benign for an opt-out round-up design.
limitations: Healthcare insurance for low-income elderly beneficiaries, not a consumer banking app
Government program with different decision stakes and reversibility than a savings feature
relevance_reason: One of the strongest persistence/passivity findings on default effects outside the pension literature, useful as an upper-bound case for how sticky default effects can be.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and auto-escalation: steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of auto-escalation defaults are kept at the first escalation date.
methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job turnover, balance withdrawal at separation, and opt-out from auto-escalation.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of our support team's objection: default enrolment's effect is much smaller once turnover, withdrawal, and later opt-out are accounted for — directly bears on whether an opt-out round-up default produces durable saving or just nominal, short-lived enrolment.
limitations: Retirement plans (401k) rather than liquid consumer savings
Employer-mediated auto-escalation mechanism does not map onto a self-directed app setting
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving, with quantified effect sizes, which the brief explicitly asked us to look for.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, but most enrollees actively opted back out, and the default effect was stronger when incentives were higher and awareness of enrollment status was lower.
methodology: Natural experiment using administrative and survey data around a national auto-enrollment policy rollout.
why_it_matters: Shows a large headline default effect (23pp) can coexist with widespread active opt-out concentrated among the less-informed, foreshadowing that our enrolment number could reflect confusion rather than genuine preference.
limitations: Public pay-as-you-go pension system, not a consumer banking app
Employer/government-mediated context
relevance_reason: A recent, large default-effect estimate with heterogeneity by knowledge/incentive, directly bearing on who a default enrolment helps versus confuses.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's gains on participation and contributions, replicated at 12 months, attenuate substantially by 36 months, though it still meaningfully lowers savings inequality; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Panel data from over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK representative panel; life-cycle consumption-savings model calibration.
why_it_matters: Quantifies exactly the decay from short-run enrolment gain to modest medium-run saving increase that the support team predicts for round-up defaults, while showing the distributional (equalizing) benefit is real even if average gains shrink.
limitations: Retirement savings plans, not liquid consumer savings
Employer/national-panel data, not a self-directed app
relevance_reason: Directly measures the medium-run attenuation of default effects the brief asks about, with a distributional finding on who benefits.

key_finding: Default nudges shift risk-taking by medium-to-large effect sizes across five European consumer samples (n=4207), but also lower how users rate the advisor's advice, especially when the default is rejected, and how the default is framed further shifts behavior.
methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative-sample experiment across five European countries, on investment/savings default framing.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can move behavior strongly while simultaneously damaging perceived trustworthiness — directly relevant to the reputational-risk concern about the round-up default reading as manipulative, and to how the multiplier field should be framed and worded.
limitations: Wealth-management investment-risk context rather than round-up savings specifically
Advice-rating measure is a proxy for trust, not actual disengagement or complaints
relevance_reason: EU consumer financial-decision experiment giving effect sizes for both the default's behavioral pull and its perceived-manipulation cost — exactly the trade-off the brief flags as a reputational risk.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment raised 401(k) participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of enrollees initially accepted both the low default contribution rate and conservative default fund, and half still did at three years, roughly offsetting the wealth gains from higher participation on average, while substantially reducing non-participation in the lower tail.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans, multi-year follow-up.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a preset default level anchors most people for years, which is the central risk in shipping a pre-set round-up multiplier rather than a blank field — later contradicting studies argue directly with this one.
limitations: Employer 401(k) plans, not a consumer app
Predates the fintech/liquid-savings and current EU regulatory context
relevance_reason: The classic study everything on default anchoring and enrollment in this list responds to; establishes the anchoring mechanism the brief worries about for the multiplier choice.

key_finding: In 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions, 84% of default adherence comes from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost, and removing either friction alone would not sustain adherence; adding an intermediate tip option captured 69% of achievable welfare gain at low revenue cost.
methodology: Structural model estimated on 8.6M transactions, validated against a stated-preference survey of true preferences.
why_it_matters: Names the specific mechanism — deviation cost plus opt-out cost — that makes any preset default 'sticky', which transfers directly to designing how easy it should be to change the round-up multiplier or exit the feature, and suggests an intermediate preset captures most of the achievable benefit cheaply.
limitations: Consumer tipping decisions, not a savings product
Single-transaction choice rather than an ongoing enrolment decision
relevance_reason: Explicit method transfer: the friction-decomposition model of why defaults stick is directly usable to reason about our opt-out design and multiplier menu, even though the tested product is a taxi tip.

key_finding: Take-up of an opt-in payroll-deduction short-term (liquid, withdraw-anytime) savings account was under 0.7% of eligible employees, but among adopters, 96% still held a balance and 87% received a contribution at month 12.
methodology: Field study of a short-term savings program introduced at five UK firms, tracked over the first 12 months.
why_it_matters: The closest real-world analogue to a round-up pot (liquid, withdrawable savings): shows opt-in produces very low headline enrolment but very high persistence among those who do enrol — a direct data point for the opt-in vs opt-out trade-off.
limitations: Employer payroll-deduction context, not a self-directed banking app
No opt-out or active-choice arm to compare against
relevance_reason: Empirically shows opt-in's enrolment cost but also its retention benefit for a liquid savings product structurally very similar to the round-up feature.

key_finding: A general theoretical characterization shows that when the designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions to cases of disagreement, externalities, and Pigouvian fees.
methodology: Theoretical model with asymptotic analysis and numerical simulations. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a normative framework for when minimizing opt-outs (defaulting people in) is actually optimal versus when disagreement about the activity's value should push toward a different default, relevant to whether opt-out is justified given heterogeneous saving preferences.
limitations: Pure theory with simulations, no empirical application to any consumer product
Abstract gives no domain-specific guidance for savings apps
relevance_reason: General normative theory of optimal defaults bearing on whether opt-out enrolment is justified when user preferences over saving are heterogeneous, which the brief's distributional question raises.

key_finding: Maps EU laws addressing dark patterns and develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from manipulation requiring regulation.
methodology: Legal/doctrinal analysis and taxonomy development; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete EU legal framework for judging whether an opt-out enrolment or a pre-selected multiplier would read as a dark pattern versus a legitimate default, directly bearing on the entry-mechanism decision and reputational/regulatory risk the brief flags.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not an empirical measurement of enrolment or amounts saved
not specific to financial products or savings apps
relevance_reason: Directly addresses when a default is manipulative under EU consumer law, the brief's central regulatory concern.

key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had opted out after 12 months (versus roughly half in plans with lower defaults), and many anchored at the unmatched, likely-suboptimal 12% rate, especially lower earners.
methodology: Administrative panel data from an employer retirement plan compared against a literature review of lower-default plans.
why_it_matters: Shows a high preset default both suppresses opt-out and anchors many participants at an economically suboptimal level, a direct caution for choosing which round-up multiplier to preselect.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed liquid consumer product
no employer-matching mechanism analogous to our product exists
relevance_reason: Quantifies default-driven anchoring at a high preset contribution level, relevant to the multiplier decision.

key_finding: Using 41 million observations, automatic (passive) contributions raised savings substantially, while subsidies requiring active choice produced only $0.01 of new saving per $1 of expenditure, because 85% of individuals are passive savers unresponsive to subsidies but moved by defaults.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data from Denmark exploiting natural variation in active vs. passive savings policies.
why_it_matters: Establishes the foundational active/passive-saver heterogeneity result that later choice-architecture debates argue with, useful for predicting who a round-up default will actually help versus who was already engaged.
limitations: Danish pension/retirement account system, not a liquid consumer savings product
predates the app-based fintech and EU regulatory context
relevance_reason: Foundational large-N evidence on default effects and saver heterogeneity that the current literature builds on.

key_finding: Proposes and field-tests 'enhanced active choice,' a modified active-choice design that highlights losses from the non-preferred option, as an alternative to automatic enrolment when defaults are infeasible or ethically fraught.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments across behavior-change domains including savings.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, field-tested design for an active-choice onboarding screen that nudges toward enrolment without a default, directly informing the entry-mechanism decision and the active-choice-vs-defaults trade-off.
limitations: abstract does not report retention or amount-saved outcomes
spans health and savings domains rather than a fintech app specifically
relevance_reason: Directly compares active choice, and an enhanced variant, against defaults, the core C6 question the brief asks.

key_finding: Synthesizes household finance evidence on savings, borrowing, and choice-architecture interventions, including how product design and defaults shape financial behavior in ways that deviate from classical models.
methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Provides broad synthesis-level context connecting choice-architecture interventions to household financial outcomes, useful background though it lacks the specific effect sizes needed to settle either design decision.
limitations: abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes
covers employer-mediated retirement contexts as much as self-directed consumer fintech
relevance_reason: The broad review candidate offering synthesis-level context on choice-architecture interventions in household finance.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrolment raised participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted low default savings rates (2-3%) and conservative default funds, with half still at the default rate after three years, so higher participation did not translate proportionally into higher savings.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking automatic-enrollment cohorts over several years.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that default-driven enrolment gains can be offset by anchoring at a low default rate, directly cautioning against a low preselected round-up multiplier and showing enrolment counts can mask stagnant amounts saved.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan, not a liquid consumer product
predates fintech app context and EU regulation
relevance_reason: Foundational evidence that default enrolment gains can be undermined by anchoring at the preset level, central to the multiplier decision.

key_finding: Randomized default enrollment in a salary-linked savings account increased participation by 40 percentage points, an effect equivalent to a 50% matching incentive, driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among employees in Afghanistan, with follow-up interventions isolating mechanisms.
why_it_matters: Explains the psychological mechanism behind default effects (present bias, cognitive cost), helping predict whether a round-up default produces genuine engagement or merely passive, disengaged enrolment.
limitations: salary-linked savings account for employees, not a self-directed consumer banking app
developing-country setting differs from the EU regulatory and liquidity context
relevance_reason: Provides mechanism-level evidence for why defaults work, informing whether the round-up default will genuinely engage users.
